paper.title: The impact of health on individual retirement plans: self-reported versus diagnostic measures
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: a longitudinal database of elderly people (Aeldredatabasen), a survey fielded and collected by SFI-SURVEY
registers.role: sample frame; outcome (planned retirement age); self-reported health; job and family characteristics
variables_mentioned: Myalgia, osteoporosis, decalcification of bones, back problems

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Patient Registry (LPR, Landspatientregister)
registers.years: somatic hospital admissions since 1977; out-patients and emergency patients and psychiatric contacts since 1995; diagnoses used are typically measured over the four years preceding each survey year

registers.role: controls: precise information on individuals' labour market characteristics, earnings, wealth, compensation rate, unemployment duration, sector, self-employment, education

linkages: survey respondents from the SFI longitudinal database of elderly people merged with longitudinal register data from 1993 to 2001

survey respondents merged to hospital discharge records in the Danish National Patient Registry, giving self-reported and physician-reported measures of the same medical conditions for the same individual

sample.universe: A representative sample of individuals born every fifth year from 1920 to 1945 (5864 individuals) interviewed face to face in 1997, of whom 79% were re-interviewed by phone in 2002; the analysis is limited to those born in 1940 and 1945
selection_rules: In 1997, a representative sample of individuals born every fifth year from 1920 to 1945, consisting of 5864 individuals, was interviewed face-to-face in their homes; the response rate was 70%
79% of the first wave respondents participated in the second wave in 2002
Limit the sample to individuals born in 1940 and 1945, i.e. people aged approximately 52 and 57 years in 1997, corresponding to 4516 person-wave observations
Restrict the sample to observations for individuals who were in the labour force in the first wave (1997)

Include only individuals who report an exact planned retirement age in the year in question; observations for individuals who retired between the two waves are included given that they report their actual retirement age
sample.n_observations: almost 3000 person-wave observations, 65% of the original sample (1565 men and 1358 women in Table I; the regressions use 1549 men and 1351 women)

construction_notes: Retirement is defined as withdrawal from the labour market: the respondent answers 'Have stopped permanently' to 'Are you on the labor market now or have you stopped working?'

Self-reported disease dummy equals one if at least one of diabetes, high blood pressure, bronchitis/asthma, osteoarthritis, myalgia, osteoporosis/decalcification of bones or back problems bothers the individual in normal everyday life; an index for the number of diseases ranges from 0 to 6

The diagnoses dummy equals one if the individual has been hospitalized for either a metabolic disorder, cardiovascular disease, lung and respiratory disease, arthritic or rheumatic disease or a disease in the musculo-skeletal system and connective tissue; diagnoses follow the ICD10 classification

Diagnoses are typically measured in the four-year period preceding the year individuals are observed either on the labour market or retired; for self-reported health, health and retirement are measured in the same wave, except for individuals retiring between wave 1 and 2 for whom health is measured in wave 1
Measurement-error reduction: only those diagnoses that involve multiple hospital discharges over the years looked at are counted
Compensation rate in year t = (potential) gross income as a pensioner in year t divided by gross income as a participant in year t-1 (see Larsen and Datta Gupta, 2004)
Where earnings is less than zero, the information is replaced by information about the surplus of the individual's own firm; earnings enters as log(earnings), the average of year t-1 and t-2
Wealth is measured in year t-1 in millions of Danish kroner

Means of the measurement-error-reduced diagnoses (men, women; standard deviations in parentheses), footnote 18: Diagnoses (0-1) 0.042 (0.20) and 0.023 (0.15); diagnoses (sum) 0.051 (0.23) and 0.029 (0.18); metabolic disorders 0.003 (0.06) and 0.004 (0.06); cardiovascular diseases 0.027 (0.16) and 0.007 (0.08); lung and respiratory diseases 0.004 (0.07) and 0.005 (0.07); arthritic and rheumatic diseases 0.004 (0.07) and 0.004 (0.07); diseases in musculo-skeletal system, etc. 0.012 (0.11) and 0.007 (0.08)
Planned retirement age is treated as a continuously distributed variable; a sensitivity analysis grouping it according to pension rules and eligibility criteria is mentioned but not reported

Attrition: 155 persons or 11.8% of wave 1 respondents dropped out between the two waves; reasons were refusals (72.3%), moved away (5.2%), could not be contacted (14.2%), emigrated (1.9%), illness (4.5%), death (1.3%)

claims.statement: Among men, being diagnosed (any of the five diagnosis groups) has no statistically significant effect on planned retirement age (Table III, Men, Without reduction; point estimate -0.268 years).

definition.value: Dummy variable set equal to one if the individual has been hospitalized for either a metabolic disorder, cardiovascular disease, lung and respiratory disease, arthritic or rheumatic disease or a disease in the musculo-skeletal system and connective tissue; the diagnoses are taken from the Danish National Patient Registry (LPR) and classified according to ICD10

timing.value: Typically measured over the four-year period preceding the year in which the individual is observed (survey wave 1997 or 2002)

definition.value: Age at which the individual reports planning to retire, taken from the 1997 and 2002 waves of the survey; retirement is defined as permanent withdrawal from the labour market. It is treated as a continuously distributed variable. Observations for individuals who retired between the two waves are included using their reported actual retirement age.

timing.value: Reported in the survey wave (1997 or 2002); for individuals who retired between the two waves the actual retirement age reported in wave 2 is used

units.value: years of planned retirement age per unit of the 0-1 diagnosis indicator

estimand.target_population: older Danish men born in 1940 or 1945 who were in the labour force in 1997 and report an exact planned retirement age
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous: planned retirement age is measured in the survey wave and the diagnosis in the four-year period preceding it

population.description: Older Danish men born in 1940 or 1945 (aged about 52 and 57 in 1997), drawn from the 1997 and 2002 waves of the SFI longitudinal database of elderly people and merged to register data, who were in the labour force in wave 1 and report an exact planned retirement age
population.ages: approximately 52 and 57 years in 1997 (57 and 62 in 2002)
population.selection: Conditioned on being in the labour force in wave 1 (1997) and on reporting an exact planned retirement age; individuals already retired in 1997 through the Social Disability Pension, early retirement or the Transitional Benefit Program are excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-person variation in register-recorded hospital diagnoses in the four years preceding each survey wave, among workers only; no reform, lottery or instrument is used. Identification rests on controlling for economic, job and background characteristics and, where indicated, on correcting for sample selection.

key_assumptions.assumption: Underlying health H is orthogonal to the disturbance of the retirement equation and to the measurement errors in the subjective and objective health measures; conditional on the 15 controls the diagnostic measure is uncorrelated with the unobserved determinants of planned retirement age.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the orthogonality assumption when setting out the empirical model and argues that justification bias cannot be present in the register measure; it offers no test of conditional ignorability.

lhs: Diagnoses (0-1)
rhs: Unobserved determinants of planned retirement age (e)
given: Log (earnings), average of year t-1 and t-2

implies_edges.from: Log (earnings), average of year t-1 and t-2

formal.as_written: Assume that H is orthogonal to e, ms and mo.

key_assumptions.assumption: Justification bias is absent in the register-based diagnostic measure: its measurement error is uncorrelated with the error of the retirement equation (unlike the survey self-report).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the construction of the measure (physician-recorded hospital discharges rather than self-report); Table II correlations are offered as suggestive support.

lhs: Measurement error in the register diagnosis (mo)
rhs: Unobserved determinants of planned retirement age (e)
formal.as_written: Justification bias will not be present with the objective measure, Ho, as mo is uncorrelated with e

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting diagnoses to those that involve multiple hospital discharges reduces the measurement error in objective health, because repeated contact with the health-care system proxies disruption to work life and productivity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of the 'without reduction' and 'with reduction' panels of Table III; the authors conclude the correction works as intended.

key_assumptions.assumption: Planned retirement age is a valid indicator of retirement behaviour.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 shows spikes at the institutional eligibility ages; Figure 2 compares the cumulative distribution of planned retirement age in wave 1 with actual retirement age in wave 2 for those who retire between waves.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on being in the labour force in wave 1 and on reporting an exact planned retirement age; the authors note the resulting sample may not be representative.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table I compares means of the working sample with those out of the labour force and those giving no exact planned retirement age; many differences are significant at the 10% level.

implies_edges.to: Sample inclusion (in the labour force in wave 1 and reports an exact planned retirement age)

threats_discussed: justification bias in survey self-reports of health
measurement error in objective health measures, which measure underlying health rather than work incapacity
heterogeneity in the propensity to go to the doctor, correlated with the propensity to work or retire
sample selection from omitting individuals already retired in 1997 (Social Disability Pension, Transitional Benefit Program)
sample selection from only including individuals who report an exact planned retirement age
health-related attrition between the two waves (footnote 8)
reverse causality from withdrawal from the labour market to health, argued to be less problematic because the measure is planned rather than actual retirement (footnote 1)
unobserved heterogeneity such as workers' time-rate of preference (footnote 2)
low incidence of diagnoses in the female sample
robustness_checks: pooled OLS with and without reduction of measurement error (Table III)
Heckman full-ML selection correction for two separate selection rules (Tables IV and V)
fixed effects Heckman two-step estimates (Appendix Table AI)
sensitivity analysis grouping planned retirement age according to pension rules and eligibility criteria (not reported)
specifications in which all diagnoses are jointly included (available on request)
interactions of each diagnostic measure with private sector and physically demanding job dummies (footnote 17)
unresolved_confounders: heterogeneity in the propensity to go to the doctor that may be correlated with the propensity to work or retire
individuals still in the labour market may also not report true health
timing mismatch between the survey measure (indefinite period) and the register measure (four preceding years)

controls: Log (earnings), average of year t-1 and t-2

heterogeneity.dimension: measurement error in the diagnostic measure
heterogeneity.finding: The same specification estimated on diagnoses restricted to those with multiple hospital discharges ('with reduction') is reported in the adjacent panel of Table III; for men the health effects become uniformly stronger and more significant.

The symmetric specification for women is estimated separately; the paper reports that more diagnoses are significantly related to retirement for men than women, but that cardiovascular disease and diseases of the musculo-skeletal system have a stronger effect on female than male retirement.

population.description: Older Danish women born in 1940 or 1945 (aged about 52 and 57 in 1997), drawn from the 1997 and 2002 waves of the SFI longitudinal database of elderly people and merged to register data, who were in the labour force in wave 1 and report an exact planned retirement age

key_assumptions.assumption: Underlying health H is orthogonal to the disturbance of the retirement equation and to the measurement errors in the subjective and objective health measures; conditional on the 15 controls the diagnostic measure is uncorrelated with the unobserved determinants of planned retirement age.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the orthogonality assumption when setting out the empirical model and argues that justification bias cannot be present in the register measure; it offers no test of conditional ignorability.
